title: Rehearse the end
hook: an old man's advice: rehearse death, so you can meet it well (Letters 26)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the water clock. Your line was notice the water running. Did you catch an hour being spent, and spend the next one on purpose? Day four hundred fifty-five.
screen: `THE WATER CLOCK — NOTICE THE WATER RUNNING.`

segments.voice: Actors rehearse the hardest scene the most. Pilots practice the engine failure in a simulator, over and over, so that on the real day their hands already know what to do. Nobody calls that morbid. It's how you get calm about something you can't avoid. In the twenty-sixth letter, Seneca is old, and he says so. His body is wearing out. And he gives Lucilius a piece of advice he borrowed, cheerfully, from a rival school. It's the one scene every one of us will play exactly once. Today, the last day of this week in the letters: rehearse the end.
screen: `PILOTS PRACTICE THE ENGINE FAILURE.` → `SENECA IS OLD, AND SAYS SO.` → `THE SCENE WE PLAY ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, the old man. Seneca writes that his body is worn, but his mind feels young and glad to have less to do with the body. Old age, he says, has taken away his vices more than his strength. Second, the examiner. He says he'll let death decide how far he has come. Talk is cheap. Anyone can sound brave in a letter. The last day will show whether his calm was real or a performance. So he prepares for it, the way a student prepares for an exam whose date is unknown. Third, the borrowed advice. It comes from Epicurus, whose school disagreed with the Stoics about a great deal. Seneca quotes him anyway: rehearse death. And he adds his own gloss: whoever tells you this is telling you to rehearse freedom. A person who has learned how to die, he says, has unlearned how to be a slave. Fear of the end is the leash that lets everything else pull us around. Fourth, our week, looked back. We started with a short walk and back to the mind, then words that shape the soul, starting poor, deeds that match words, real joy, the water clock, and now this. Every one asks the same thing: do you live it, or only say it? Rehearsing the end asks it where it's hardest to fake.
screen: `AN OLD BODY, A YOUNG MIND.` · `LET DEATH BE THE EXAMINER.` · `REHEARSE DEATH: REHEARSE FREEDOM.` · `THE WEEK: LIVE IT, NOT ONLY SAY IT.` · then, large: `READY, CALMLY.`

segments.voice: This is gentle. If today is a hard day for this, simply rest with your breath instead. Otherwise, sit comfortably and let the thought arrive: one day, I'll end. Don't picture how. Just let the fact be in the room, the way Seneca does in this letter. Notice what your body does. Then ask quietly: if that day came, what would I want to have done, said, set right? Let one answer surface. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Meditare mortem. Epicurus' advice, which Seneca borrows: rehearse death, because whoever has learned to die has unlearned slavery. Today's word.

Your line: ready, calmly. Take the one answer that surfaced, the thing you'd want done or said, and do a small piece of it today. That's our week in Seneca's letters. Next week, more letters. Day four hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: Stoic practitioners sometimes keep a brief, calm reflection on their own mortality, often in the evening, and use it to set right something they would not want left undone.

original.note: Latin, Seneca's rendering of Epicurus in Letters 26.8: rehearse (practice, think on) death.

trapdoor: what you thought: thinking about death is morbid.
what it means: rehearsing the end calmly loosens fear's leash on the rest of life.

what a scholar hears: Letters 26.8–10, 'meditare mortem' from Epicurus, and 'qui mori didicit servire dedidicit'; the Stoic and Epicurean schools disagreed on much, yet Seneca quotes Epicurus here without apology.
